title: The Center of the Earth and the Count of Stars (MR)
summary: A conceited philosopher asks Birbal to identify the center of the earth and the number of hairs on a sheep. Birbal silences him with effortless precision.
full_text:
A haughty philosopher from Shiraz arrived at the imperial court of Agra, boasting that no scholar in the East could match his cosmological knowledge. Standing before Emperor Akbar, the philosopher posed two challenge questions:

'Tell me, Raja Birbal: what is the exact center of the earth? And how many stars shine in the heavens? Answer with precision, or admit your ignorance!'

The assembled courtiers held their breath. These were impossible cosmological questions!

Birbal smiled calmly, walked to the center of the marble hall, and drove an iron-tipped royal staff into a seam between two floor stones.

'Here,' Birbal declared, pointing to the staff. 'This exact spot where my staff stands is the precise center of the earth! If you doubt my calculation, noble philosopher, take a measuring rope, measure around the globe in every direction, and if you find it off by even one millimeter, I shall forfeit my life!'

The philosopher coughed nervously, unable to dispute the claim without measuring the entire earth.

'And the stars in heaven?' the philosopher demanded, trying to recover his pride.

Birbal immediately ordered a royal shepherd to bring a colossal, fluffy white sheep into the hall.

Birbal gestured to the animal: 'Sir, there are exactly as many stars in the heavens as there are hairs upon the body of this sheep! If you doubt my count, please step forward and count the hairs on this sheep, and then count the stars, and see if they do not match with absolute perfection!'

The philosopher turned red with embarrassment: 'How can anyone count the hairs of a sheep?'

'Just as easily as one can count the stars in heaven!' Birbal retorted, his eyes dancing with humor.

The Persian scholar bowed in defeat, praising Birbal for proving that unanswerable riddles can only be resolved by showing the absurdity of the question itself.
